name: Hereditary spastic paraplegia type 20 (SPG20, Troyer syndrome)

clinicalPearls: Autosomal recessive complicated hereditary spastic paraplegia first characterised in the Old Order Amish, caused by loss-of-function mutations in SPART, which encodes spartin.
The hallmark is childhood-onset spastic paraparesis combined with distal muscle wasting (amyotrophy), which distinguishes it from pure hereditary spastic paraplegias.
Additional features include short stature, dysarthria, drooling, pseudobulbar emotional lability and mild learning difficulty.
Cerebellar signs and distal skeletal changes of the hands and feet may accompany the picture.
A founder frameshift mutation predominates in the Amish, but the syndrome occurs in other populations with different SPART variants, so ancestry should not gate testing.
Progression is slow; many patients reach adult life but accumulate disability and may lose independent ambulation.
MRI may show cerebral or cerebellar atrophy and non-specific white-matter change and is supportive rather than diagnostic.
reference.pathophysiology: SPART encodes spartin, a multifunctional protein carrying an MIT (microtubule-interacting and trafficking) domain that participates in endosomal trafficking and receptor turnover, downregulation of bone morphogenetic protein signalling, turnover of cytoplasmic lipid droplets, and mitochondrial calcium handling and quality control. Truncating loss-of-function mutations abolish spartin, and the combined disturbance of endosomal sorting, lipid metabolism and mitochondrial maintenance preferentially injures the longest central motor axons, producing the corticospinal-tract degeneration responsible for spasticity, while accompanying anterior-horn and peripheral involvement contributes to the characteristic distal amyotrophy. The broader developmental features of short stature, cognitive involvement and cerebellar signs reflect spartin's wider roles beyond the corticospinal tract. This places Troyer syndrome among the complicated recessive hereditary spastic paraplegias in which membrane-trafficking and organelle-maintenance pathways are disrupted.
additionalDifferentials: Other complicated recessive hereditary spastic paraplegias (SPG11, SPG15, SPG7)
Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease with pyramidal signs, given the distal amyotrophy
Spastic diplegia labelled as cerebral palsy
Other syndromic short-stature and neurodevelopmental disorders
additionalInvestigations: SPART sequencing and dosage analysis within a recessive hereditary spastic paraplegia or exome panel
MRI brain and spine for cerebral/cerebellar atrophy and white-matter change
Nerve conduction studies and EMG to characterise the amyotrophy
Assessment of growth, bone age and a skeletal survey for short stature and skeletal change
Documentation of consanguinity and family history, with carrier testing of relatives
Screening for treatable mimics as clinically indicated
redFlags: Aspiration arising from bulbar or pseudobulbar dysfunction
Rapidly progressive weakness suggesting a motor neuron process
Failure to thrive or severe growth failure requiring endocrine review
Marked cognitive regression, prompting reassessment of the diagnosis
reference.prognosis: Slowly progressive; distal wasting and spasticity worsen through adolescence and adulthood with eventual loss of independent walking in many patients, although survival into mid-adult life and beyond is usual.
pitfalls: Mistaking the distal amyotrophy for Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease and missing the complicated pyramidal picture
Labelling childhood spasticity as cerebral palsy without genetic testing
Expecting all cases to be of Amish ancestry and not testing SPART in other populations
Interpreting non-specific MRI change as excluding the diagnosis
management: No disease-specific therapy exists; treat spasticity with oral antispasticity agents such as baclofen or tizanidine and focal botulinum toxin, with intrathecal baclofen reserved for refractory tone
Physiotherapy, stretching, orthoses and orthopaedic input for spasticity and distal amyotrophy, with hand and foot care
Speech and language therapy plus saliva-control measures such as antimuscarinic agents or botulinum toxin to the salivary glands for dysarthria and drooling
Consider antidepressant therapy and psychological support for pseudobulbar emotional lability
Educational and neuropsychological support for mild learning difficulty, with growth monitoring for short stature
Genetic counselling with cascade SPART testing for autosomal recessive inheritance, offered regardless of ancestry
Escalate to multidisciplinary rehabilitation as ambulation declines through adolescence and adulthood
